auxiliary_material: The authors demonstrate the biological relevance of inosine quantification by showing that converting adenosine to inosine within the tumor microenvironment (TME) reverses immunosuppression. Mechanistically, increased inosine correlated with enhanced CD8+ T cell infiltration, a shift from M2 to M1 macrophage phenotypes, and upregulation of cytokines (IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-12p70). The study also validates that inosine can serve as an alternative carbon source for T cells under glucose-depleted conditions, supporting the rationale for monitoring these metabolites in cancer contexts.

The study provides mechanistic context linking microbial inosine biosynthesis to CAR T-cell cytotoxicity via the adenosine A2A receptor, and links SCFA-producing bacteria to reduced toxicity. Review planning notes highlight that while the study focuses on CAR T-cell therapy in blood cancer, the metabolic pathways (inosine, SCFAs) and toxicity associations (isovalerate) offer comparative material for understanding microbiome-immune interactions in broader immunotherapy contexts. The authors note limitations including sample size, the exploratory nature of metabolite analyses, and the use of in vitro inosine concentrations exceeding physiological levels.

The specific GC–MS analytical parameters (e.g., column type, temperature program, ionization settings) were not disclosed in the text as the analysis was outsourced to a commercial vendor (Suzhou Meixin Bioscience Co., Ltd). The study focused on acetic acid and did not address inosine quantification. No absolute concentration values or established reference ranges for clinical application were provided in the text, only relative quantification or graphical representation of accumulation. The study design is experimental rather than a methodological guideline or consensus statement.

outline_action: Use the reported LC-MS/MS parameters and SPME extraction technique as a preclinical example of technical feasibility for inosine quantification in solid tumors. Cite the observed murine baseline concentrations to illustrate typical orders of magnitude in tumor tissue, while explicitly distinguishing these from human reference ranges. Leverage the mechanistic findings (adenosine-to-inosine conversion effects on immunity) to justify the need for standardized human quantification protocols in the review, but note that the specific success criteria for human consensus and reference ranges remain unfulfilled by this source.

query_audits.query_text: inosine short-chain fatty acids LC-MS/MS GC-MS quantification protocol human serum tumor microenvironment reference range

Are there established standardized measurement protocols or consensus guidelines for absolute quantification of inosine and short-chain fatty acids in human cancer patient serum or tumor tissue samples?

remaining_gap: The supplied material does not provide standardized analytical protocols for human serum or tumor tissue, as all quantification was performed in murine models (MC38 colorectal cancer). There are no human-specific reference concentration ranges for inosine or short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in cancer patients or healthy controls. Furthermore, the paper does not address SCFA quantification methods at all, nor does it cite or establish any consensus guidelines for clinical metabolite monitoring.
useful_material: This study details a specific LC-MS/MS method for quantifying inosine and adenosine in tumor tissue, utilizing an Agilent 1290 Infinity II UHPLC coupled to a 6475 Triple Quad mass spectrometer in positive MRM mode. Key parameters include a ZORBAX RRHD Eclipse Plus C18 column (150 mm × 3 mm, 1.8 µm), a water (0.1% formic acid)/acetonitrile gradient at 300 µL/min, and specific parent/product ion pairs for inosine (269.1/136.8) and adenosine (268.1/135.9). Sample processing employed hydrophilic-lipophilic balanced solid-phase microextraction (HLB-SPME) fibers inserted directly into murine tumors, with lamivudine as an internal standard. The authors reported a baseline adenosine concentration of approximately 0.04 µM in control mouse tumor tissue.

This study confirms the use of liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) for quantifying serum short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and inosine in patients with relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma undergoing CAR T-cell therapy. The authors report that detailed analytical procedures are described in supplemental methods, though these are not included in the supplied text. The study identifies associations between serum inosine levels and treatment response, and between specific serum fatty acids (acetate, butyrate, isovalerate) and immune-related adverse events. It establishes that these metabolites are measurable in human serum within a cancer immunotherapy context.

This study utilized gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) to quantify short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), specifically acetic acid, in human lung adenocarcinoma tissues (n = 21) and adjacent normal tissues. The authors reported sample processing standards including tissue dissection, washing with precooled PBS, and storage at −80 °C prior to analysis. The results indicated a significant accumulation of acetic acid in tumor tissues compared to normal tissues, supporting the feasibility of SCFA quantification in tumor samples for cancer research.
